narrative.text: Front cover of the WHO publication Classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health: a shared language to describe the uses of digital technology for health, second edition (v2.0).

Presents a comprehensive visual reference chart of the entire second-edition classification across all three axes: Digital Health Interventions (1.0 Persons, 2.0 Healthcare Providers, 3.0 Health Management and Support Personnel, 4.0 Data Services), Health System Challenges (categories 1–9), and Services and Application Types (categories A–E).
Inner title page for Classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health: a shared language to describe the uses of digital technology for health, second edition.

Provides bibliographic metadata (ISBN 978-92-4-008194-9 electronic / 978-92-4-008195-6 print), a note on the retitling from the 2018 first edition (WHO/RHR/18.06), 2023 WHO copyright and CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO licensing terms, suggested citation, third-party material terms, and general disclaimers.

Table of contents listing the front matter, introductory overview, Health System Challenges, the four Digital Health Intervention groups, Digital Services and Application Types, References, and Annex.

Acknowledges the WHO Department of Digital Health and Innovation and Department of Reproductive Health and Research coordination team, the Classifications Advisory Committee, the Classifications Small Working Group, first-edition contributors, and funding partners (Fondation Botnar, Rockefeller Foundation, HRP, USAID, and CDC).

Executive summary defining digital health, explaining the rationale for updating the 2018 classification into the three-axis Classification of Digital Interventions, Services and Applications in Health (CDISAH), and summarizing the structural updates—most notably replacing Systems Categories with restructured Services and Application Types.

Summarizes the major content changes in the second edition—shifting from 'Client(s)' to 'Person(s)' or 'Individual(s)', adding pandemic-era and emerging DHIs, expanding descriptors and synonyms, and organizing Services and Application Types into five architectural representations—accompanied by the complete classification overview chart.

Introduces the purpose and audience of the Classification of Digital Interventions, Services and Applications in Health (CDISAH), reviews the four foundational use cases that motivated the first edition alongside technical standards (COBIT, HL7, ISO), and lists ten current global applications of the classification.

Explains how the CDISAH is organized across its three axes—nine Health System Challenge categories, four primary-user DHI groupings (Persons, Healthcare Providers, Health Management and Support Personnel, and Data Services) with synonyms and examples, and five architectural representations of Services and Application Types—and introduces how to use them together.

Explains how to pair Digital Health Interventions with Health System Challenges and Services and Application Types to support planning and interoperability, illustrated by Figure 1 mapping specific challenges (such as commodity shortages or loss to follow-up) to DHIs and system types (such as LMIS, EMR, and HMIS).

Presents four practical use cases for the classification: (1) selecting DHIs to address a health system challenge such as missed newborn immunizations, (2) articulating the DHIs delivered by a digital therapeutic application, (3) conducting landscape analyses of digital health investments, and (4) searching registered projects in the WHO Digital Health Atlas.

Highlights three related WHO companion publications (the WHO digital health guideline, the Digital Implementation Investment Guide, and the DIIG quick deployment guide), defines three core terms (digital health intervention, digital health application, and health system challenge), and lists six introductory references.
Transition page displaying the running footer and navigation tabs for the six main sections of the WHO Classification v2.0.
Part divider page introducing the main body of Digital Interventions, Services and Applications in Health.

Section divider introducing the Health System Challenges framework as a standardized starting point for program planners to identify bottlenecks in health programme processes and select appropriate digital health interventions.

Presents the complete Health System Challenges taxonomy across nine categories: 1 Information (1.1–1.7), 2 Availability (2.1–2.4), 3 Quality (3.1–3.8), 4 Acceptability (4.1–4.2), 5 Utilization (5.1–5.4), 6 Efficiency (6.1–6.6), 7 Cost (7.1–7.4), 8 Accountability (8.1–8.6), and 9 Equity (9.1–9.2).
Section divider introducing Group 1.0 (Digital Health Interventions for Persons), covering members of the public who are potential or current users of health services as well as their caregivers.

Presents the taxonomy tree for Group 1.0 (Digital Health Interventions for Persons) across eight categories: 1.1 Targeted communication to persons (1.1.1–1.1.4), 1.2 Untargeted communication to persons (1.2.1–1.2.2), 1.3 Person-to-person communication (1.3.1), 1.4 Personal health tracking (1.4.1–1.4.4), 1.5 Person-based reporting (1.5.1–1.5.2), 1.6 On-demand communication with persons (1.6.1–1.6.2), 1.7 Person-centred financial transactions (1.7.1–1.7.3), and 1.8 Person-centred consent management (1.8.1).

Details Category 1.1 (Targeted communication to Persons) with semantically related descriptors and representative examples for 1.1.1 Transmit health event alerts to specific population groups, 1.1.2 Transmit targeted health information based on health status or demographics, and 1.1.3 Transmit targeted alerts and reminders to persons.

Concludes Category 1.1 with 1.1.4 (Transmit diagnostics result, or availability of result, to persons) and details Category 1.2 (Untargeted communication to Persons: 1.2.1 untargeted health information and 1.2.2 untargeted health event alerts) and Category 1.3 (Person to Person communication: 1.3.1 Peer group for individuals).

Details Category 1.4 (Personal health tracking) with descriptors and representative examples for 1.4.1 Access by the individual to own medical or summary health records, 1.4.2 Self-monitoring of health or diagnostic data, 1.4.3 Active data capture/documentation by an individual, and 1.4.4 Access by the individual to verifiable documentation of a health event or health status.

Details Category 1.5 (Person-based reporting: 1.5.1 Reporting of health system feedback by persons and 1.5.2 Reporting of public health events by persons) and Category 1.6 (On-demand communication with persons: 1.6.1 Look-up of information on health and health services and 1.6.2 Simulated human-like conversations with individuals, including chatbots).

Details Category 1.7 (Person-centred financial transactions: 1.7.1 out-of-pocket payments, 1.7.2 vouchers, and 1.7.3 incentives for health services) and Category 1.8 (Person-centred consent management: 1.8.1 Manage provision and withdrawal of consent by individuals).
Section divider introducing Group 2.0 (Digital Health Interventions for Healthcare Providers), covering members of the health workforce who deliver health interventions.

Presents the taxonomy tree for Group 2.0 (Digital Health Interventions for Healthcare Providers) across eleven categories: 2.1 Identification and registration of persons, 2.2 Person-centred health records, 2.3 Healthcare provider decision support, 2.4 Telemedicine, 2.5 Healthcare provider communication (including 2.5.6 Generative AI for tailored content creation), 2.6 Referral coordination, 2.7 Scheduling and activity planning, 2.8 Healthcare provider training, 2.9 Prescription and medication management, 2.10 Laboratory and diagnostics imaging management, and 2.11 Healthcare provider financial transactions.

Details Category 2.1 (Identification and registration of persons: 2.1.1 Verify a person's unique identity and 2.1.2 Enrol persons for health services/clinical care plan) and introduces Category 2.2 (Person-centred health records) with 2.2.1 Longitudinal tracking of a person's health status and services.

Continues Category 2.2 with 2.2.2 (Manage person-centred structured clinical records), 2.2.3 (Manage person-centred unstructured clinical records), and 2.2.4 (Routine health indicator data collection and management), and introduces Category 2.3 (Healthcare provider decision support) with 2.3.1 (Provide prompts and alerts based according to protocol) and 2.3.2 (Provide checklist according to protocol).

Concludes Category 2.3 with 2.3.3 (Screen persons by risk or other health status) and details Category 2.4 (Telemedicine): 2.4.1 Consultations between remote person and healthcare provider, 2.4.2 Remote monitoring of person's health or diagnostic data by provider, 2.4.3 Transmission of medical data to healthcare provider, and 2.4.4 Consultations for case management between healthcare providers.

Details Category 2.5 (Healthcare provider communication): 2.5.1 Communication from healthcare provider to supervisors, 2.5.2 Communication and performance feedback to healthcare providers, 2.5.3 Transmit routine news and workflow notifications, 2.5.4 Transmit non-routine health event alerts, 2.5.5 Peer group for healthcare providers, and 2.5.6 Generative AI for tailored content creation.

Details Category 2.6 (Referral coordination: 2.6.1 Coordinate emergency response and transport, 2.6.2 Manage referrals within the health sector, and 2.6.3 Manage referrals between health and other sectors) and introduces Category 2.7 (Scheduling and activity planning for healthcare providers) with 2.7.1 Identify persons in need of services.

Concludes Category 2.7 with 2.7.2 (Schedule healthcare provider's activities), details Category 2.8 (Healthcare provider training: 2.8.1 Provide training content and 2.8.2 Assess capacity of healthcare providers), and introduces Category 2.9 (Prescription and medication management) with 2.9.1 (Transmit or track prescription orders) and 2.9.2 (Track individual's medication consumption).

Concludes Category 2.9 with 2.9.3 (Report adverse drug effects) and details Category 2.10 (Laboratory and diagnostics imaging management): 2.10.1 Transmit person's diagnostic result to healthcare provider, 2.10.2 Transmit and track diagnostic orders, 2.10.3 Capture diagnostic results from digital devices, and 2.10.4 Track biological specimens.

Details Category 2.11 (Healthcare provider financial transactions) with semantically related descriptors and representative examples for 2.11.1 Verify individual's health coverage and financing scheme membership and 2.11.2 Receive payments from individuals.

Section divider introducing Group 3.0 (Digital Health Interventions for Health Management and Support Personnel / Health System Managers), covering personnel involved in the administration and oversight of health systems.

Presents the taxonomy tree for Group 3.0 (Digital Health Interventions for Health Management and Support Personnel) across eight categories: 3.1 Human resource management (3.1.1–3.1.5), 3.2 Supply chain management (3.2.1–3.2.6), 3.3 Public health event notification (3.3.1), 3.4 Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) (3.4.1–3.4.2), 3.5 Health system financial management (3.5.1–3.5.8), 3.6 Equipment and asset management (3.6.1–3.6.2), 3.7 Facility management (3.7.1–3.7.2), and 3.8 Person-centred health certificate management (3.8.1–3.8.3).

Details Category 3.1 (Human resource management) with descriptors and representative examples for 3.1.1 List health workforce cadres and related identification information, 3.1.2 Monitor performance of healthcare provider(s), 3.1.3 Manage registration/certification of healthcare provider(s), and 3.1.4 Record training credentials of healthcare provider(s).

Concludes Category 3.1 with 3.1.5 (Manage health workforce activities) and introduces Category 3.2 (Supply chain management) with 3.2.1 Manage inventory and distribution of health commodities, 3.2.2 Notify stock levels of health commodities, 3.2.3 Monitor cold-chain sensitive commodities, and 3.2.4 Register licensed drugs and health commodities.

Concludes Category 3.2 with 3.2.5 (Manage procurement of commodities) and 3.2.6 (Report counterfeit or substandard drugs by persons), and details Category 3.3 (Public health event notification: 3.3.1 Notification of public health events from point of diagnosis) and Category 3.4 (Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS): 3.4.1 Notify, register and certify birth event and 3.4.2 Notify, register and certify death event).

Introduces Category 3.5 (Health system financial management) with descriptors and representative examples for 3.5.1 Register and verify health coverage scheme membership of persons, 3.5.2 Track and manage insurance billing and claims processes, 3.5.3 Transmit and manage payments to health facilities, 3.5.4 Transmit and manage routine payroll payment to healthcare provider(s), and 3.5.5 Transmit or manage financial incentives to healthcare provider(s).

Concludes Category 3.5 with 3.5.6 (Manage and plan budget allocations, revenue and expenditures), 3.5.7 (Determine level of subsidies for health coverage schemes), and 3.5.8 (Collect health insurance contributions), and details Category 3.6 (Equipment and asset management: 3.6.1 Monitor status and maintenance of health equipment and 3.6.2 Track regulation and licensing of medical equipment).

Details Category 3.7 (Facility management: 3.7.1 List health facilities and related information and 3.7.2 Assess health facilities) and Category 3.8 (Person-centred health certificate management: 3.8.1 Register and store current health certificate information, 3.8.2 Retrieve and validate current health certificate information, and 3.8.3 Revoke and update health certificate).
Section divider introducing Group 4.0 (Digital Health Interventions for Data Services), covering digital technology capabilities that support optimal data management, use, and governance.

Presents the taxonomy tree for Group 4.0 (Digital Health Interventions for Data Services) across five categories: 4.1 Data Management (4.1.1–4.1.4), 4.2 Data coding (4.2.1–4.2.3), 4.3 Geo spatial information management (4.3.1–4.3.5), 4.4 Data exchange and Interoperability (4.4.1–4.4.3), and 4.5 Data governance compliance (4.5.1–4.5.4).

Details Category 4.1 (Data Management) with descriptors and representative examples for 4.1.1 Form creation for data acquisition, 4.1.2 Data storage and aggregation, 4.1.3 Data synthesis and visualizations, and 4.1.4 Automated analysis of data to generate new information or predictions on future events.

Details Category 4.2 (Data coding: 4.2.1 Parse unstructured data into structured data, 4.2.2 Merge, de-duplicate and curate coded datasets or terminologies, and 4.2.3 Classify disease codes or cause of mortality) and introduces Category 4.3 (Geo spatial information management) with 4.3.1 Map location of health facilities/structures and households and 4.3.2 Map location of health event.

Concludes Category 4.3 with 4.3.3 (Map location of persons and settlements), 4.3.4 (Map location of healthcare provider(s)), and 4.3.5 (Map health and health indicator data to geographic data), and details Category 4.4 (Data exchange and Interoperability: 4.4.1 Point-to-point data integration, 4.4.2 Standards-compliant interoperability, and 4.4.3 Message routing).

Details Category 4.5 (Data governance compliance) with descriptors and representative examples for 4.5.1 Authentication and authorisation, 4.5.2 Data privacy protection, 4.5.3 Data consent and provenance, and 4.5.4 Trust architecture.

Presents the overview and taxonomy tree for Services and Application Types across five architectural representations: A. Point of service (A1–A9), B. Health system/Provider administration (B1–B8), C. Registries & Directories (C1–C11), D. Data Management services (D1–D8), and E. Surveillance and Response (E1–E2).

Introduces Group A (Point of service systems) and defines A1 Communication systems, A2 Community-based information systems, A3 Decision support systems, and A4 Diagnostics information systems, listing alternative descriptors and functional areas.

Concludes Group A (Point of service systems) by defining A5 Electronic medical record systems, A6 Laboratory information systems, A7 Personal health records, A8 Pharmacy information systems, and A9 Telehealth systems, with descriptors and functional areas.

Introduces Group B (Health System/Provider administration systems) and defines B1 Blood bank information management systems, B2 Health finance-related information systems, B3 Health program monitoring systems, and B4 Human resource information systems.

Concludes Group B (Health System/Provider administration systems) by defining B5 Learning and training systems, B6 Logistics management information systems (LMIS), B7 Patient Administration systems, and B8 Research information systems, with descriptors and functional areas.

Introduces Group C (Registries & Directories) as canonical master lists and defines C1 Census and population information systems, C2 Civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems, C3 Facility management information systems, C4 (Health) Facility registries, and C5 Health worker registry.

Concludes Group C (Registries & Directories) by defining C6 Identification registries and directories, C7 Immunisation information systems, C8 Master patient index, C9 Product catalogues, C10 Public Key directories, and C11 Terminology and classification systems.

Introduces Group D (Data Management services) as validated data repositories and defines D1 Analytics systems, D2 Data interchange and interoperability, D3 Data warehouses, and D4 Environmental monitoring systems (EMIS), with descriptors and functional areas.

Concludes Group D (Data Management services) by defining D5 Geographic information systems (GIS), D6 Health Management Information systems (HMIS), D7 Knowledge management systems, and D8 Shared Health Record and Health Information Repository.

Details Group E (Surveillance and Response systems), defining E1 Emergency preparedness and response systems and E2 Public health and disease surveillance systems with alternative descriptors and functional areas.
Lists bibliographic references 1 through 26 supporting the definitions and illustrative project examples of digital health interventions across the classification.

Continues the numbered reference list for digital health interventions with citations 27 through 53, covering global eHealth surveys, mobile health monitoring, teledermatology, CHW performance feedback, adverse drug reaction reporting, health insurance systems, HRIS, and logistics software.

Concludes the numbered reference list for digital health interventions with citations 54 through 76, covering CRVS monitoring, electronic claims processing, mobile money, facility registries, digital COVID certificates, clinical coding, GIS vaccination tracking, HIE standards, and dynamic consent management.

Lists bibliographic references 1 through 15 supporting the definitions of Digital Services and Application Types, citing the WHO DIIG, EU MDR/IVDR software guidance, ONC telehealth definitions, OpenHIE architecture, CRVS, World Bank ID4D, CDC IIS, NIST, EMIS, UNICEF GIS, ISO/IEC standards, and the WHO Health EDRM glossary.
Section divider page introducing the Annex.

Annex describing how the first (2018) and second (2023) editions of the CDISAH were developed through technical consultations, gap assessments, and public feedback, stating the five guiding principles used by WHO's Department of Digital Health and Innovation for the update, and explaining how future editions will evolve.
Inside back cover page with no body text.
Back cover page of the WHO Classification of digital interventions, services and applications in health (second edition) with no extracted body text.
